西庫排笛主要出現在安地斯的西庫里音樂中，尤其與科利亞蘇尤、的的喀喀湖一帶的艾馬拉: The siku appears mainly in the sikuri music of the Andes, and is especially associated with Qullasuyu and the Aymara-speaking areas around Lake Titicaca. Traditionally two players each hold one row of pipes and alternate the notes of the scale, making interlocking melodies and a stereo effect; village ensembles still keep this way of playing. Today it is also common for one person to play both rows at once, standardised to fit Western music. The source mentions no specific composer or piece.
西庫排笛具有溫潤而富有民族特色的音色。其音域跨越中高音區，音質溫和柔和，帶有輕微: The siku has a warm timbre full of national character. Its range spans the middle and upper register, the tone is gentle and soft with a slight nasal quality, and it gives off a strong flavour of the Andes. The instrument resonates through the vibration of several bamboo pipes together, so the sound has depth and a sense of space. The bass pipes give a deep warm sound, the treble pipes a clear bright one, and the contrast in timbre is rich. Beside the transverse flute the siku sounds warmer and more inward; beside the recorder it sounds more penetrating and more strongly national. Its particular sound can make a quiet, mysterious atmosphere, and it is often used to express the calm of nature and human feeling.
The siku is the traditional panpipe of the Andes, an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.112.11. It is made of two rows of pipes, and the scale can only be completed by alternating between them; traditionally two players each hold one row, and today one person often plays both rows at once. It is used mainly for sikuri music, traditionally found in the Andes, especially in Aymara-speaking areas and around Lake Titicaca. Women used to play it from the hillsides, in groups, and it was also used to lure wild goats.
西庫排笛的管體通常以竹筍製成，也曾使用禿鷹羽毛、骨頭及其他材料。不同竹材會影響音: The pipes of the siku are usually made from bamboo cane, and vulture feathers, bone and other materials have also been used. The kind of bamboo affects the timbre: thin-walled bamboo is louder and resonates more, but it is seldom used because it breaks easily. The antara is traditionally made from a reed that grows in the "eyebrow of the forest" zone, and the pipes are lashed with one or two strips of bamboo into a raft-like trapezoid. Some forms fit an open reed pipe at the front to change the timbre, and the rectangular form has a plug inside each pipe to adjust the resonating length. The source does not state the materials of the other parts.
西庫排笛起源於秘魯與玻利維亞的艾馬拉語地區，傳統上分布於安地斯山脈，尤以的的喀喀: The siku originated in the Aymara-speaking areas of Peru and Bolivia and is traditionally spread through the Andes, most characteristically around Lake Titicaca. Because the mountain terrain is so broken, each community developed its own tuning, shape, size and playing style. The largest early instruments covered a complete scale but were too big to handle, so two people would each hold a smaller instrument and alternate, keeping the melody continuous; women also played different melodies in groups that fitted together into a complete phrase. Modern versions have been standardised for Western music, which changed the traditional form and the way of playing.
